framing: Exact words and meaning fail in different places
paragraphs: Luna can ask for the policy by its code, KROT-14, or describe it as a way to refresh an expired machine credential. Both requests want the same rule, in entirely different language. A useful retriever has to serve both, and it must keep old and restricted records out of the results either way.

Word matching makes exact terms count. Vector search compares learned representations of meaning. They tend to fail on different queries, so running both gives the right passage two chances. It also raises a new question: how much should each list count when you merge them?

We build the answer from arithmetic you can check. You will look at text analysis and BM25, place a hand-written query vector beside three passage vectors, then run a real embedding model and see how much messier it is. You will look inside the two vector indexes that make dense search fast. Then you merge the rankings, and a deliberately awkward case shows a distractor that both lists like beating the rule you need.
You end with a shortlist you can measure at each step, carrying the source identities and permissions from earlier chapters.
outcomes: Explain how BM25 and a real embedding model respond to codes and paraphrases.
Choose between HNSW and IVF, and tune the setting that trades recall for time.
Compute reciprocal-rank contributions, and measure recall per lane and at the fused cutoff.
question: Where can a governing rule disappear between two successful searches and the final shortlist?
